title: ETFs as a controlled window into private credit during liquidity stress
summary: Fears of stress in private credit markets are rising as investors assess liquidity risk during periods of redemption pressure, coinciding with the emergence of private credit ETFs following SEC approval of the first such product in early 2025. The article explores how ETF wrappers provide controlled exposure to private credit (capped at 35% allocation) while offering daily liquidity, contrasting with traditional private credit funds that may restrict withdrawals during stress.
key_points: SEC approved first private credit-branded ETF (State Street's PRIV) in February 2025, representing the first time less-liquid bond markets have been included in ETF structures for retail access
ETFs investing in private credit are limited to a maximum of 35% direct exposure to the asset class, providing controlled rather than concentrated exposure
VanEck BDC Income ETF (BIZD) with $1.5 billion AUM is down 13% year-to-date, with Blue Owl shares (a top holding) down over 46% this year
State Street's private credit ETFs (PRIV at $831M AUM, PRSD at $48M AUM) hold slightly over 20% of assets in Apollo-sourced investments
Both PRIV and PRSD have seen relatively flat performance since the beginning of 2025; BIZD traded at a discount to NAV 37 times in calendar year 2025

The primary systemic risk identified is the asset-liability mismatch (liquidity mismatch) inherent in private credit funds—private credit funds restrict redemptions while ETFs allow continuous daily trading
why_it_matters: This article illuminates how ETF structures are being used to provide controlled access to private credit markets, which have historically been inaccessible to retail investors due to illiquidity and opacity. The structural contrast between gated private credit funds (protecting against runs but limiting exit) and ETF wrappers (providing daily liquidity at potentially discounted prices) represents a market structure evolution with implications for price discovery, liquidity provisioning, and systemic risk absorption. Investors watching for signs of private credit stress now have a new tool—ETF pricing and discount/premium dynamics—to monitor market conditions in near-real-time.
macro_context: Market volatility is pushing investors toward shorter-duration bonds and risk reduction, with ETF flows reflecting flight from longer-duration fixed income into more defensive positioning. Private credit refinancing risk at higher rates represents a longer-horizon concern as asset-liability mismatches surface.
market_structure_context: ETF wrappers provide daily liquidity and real-time price adjustments for private credit exposure, contrasting with traditional private credit fund structures that restrict withdrawals during stress. This represents a structural change in how liquidity risk is managed and how markets can absorb shocks—ETF prices can reflect stress as it develops while maintaining functioning markets, whereas gated funds absorb stress more gradually but with less transparency. The 35% cap on private credit allocation in ETFs represents a structural safeguard limiting direct exposure. Both approaches aim to prevent disorderly outcomes through different mechanisms.
